cases.subject: History
cases.wording:
1. Name a job a Victorian child did.
2. Describe one difficult working condition in that job.
3. Why did many poorer families need their children's earnings?

cases.subject: History
cases.wording:
1. For example, working in a coal mine.
2. Mine work could involve darkness, long hours and danger.
3. Families needed the money for food and other necessities.

cases.subject: History
cases.wording: Teacher says: Last lesson you looked at children's working conditions. Think of one actual job, not just the word work. What did that child have to do? Now think about the family. Working could be dangerous and tiring, but losing the money could mean less food. Keep both things in mind today: protecting children was important, and changing their lives took more than telling them to stop working.

cases.subject: History
cases.wording: Parliament: Parliament debates proposed laws and decides whether to pass them.

cases.subject: History
cases.wording: law: A law is a rule that people in a country must follow.

cases.subject: History
cases.beat: Could Parliament shorten the working day?
cases.wording: Lord Shaftesbury campaigned with others to protect children through laws.

cases.subject: History
cases.beat: Could Parliament shorten the working day?
cases.wording: He was a member of Parliament, known then as Lord Ashley. Some owners opposed shorter hours because they feared losing money. Parliament made changes in stages.

cases.subject: History
cases.beat: Could Parliament shorten the working day?
cases.wording:
Modern summary of the Factory Acts:
1833: Children under nine were barred from most textile factories. Children could not work at night, and four inspectors could check the rules.
1847: A new law brought a ten-hour limit for women and young people aged 13 to 17 in textile factories.
1850: Another law fixed the times of day when these workers could work, making it harder for owners to get round the rules.

cases.subject: History
cases.beat: Could Parliament shorten the working day?
cases.wording: Why would a law need someone to check it?

cases.subject: History
cases.beat: Could Parliament shorten the working day?
cases.wording: Lord Shaftesbury campaigned with others to protect children through laws.

cases.subject: History
cases.beat: Could Parliament shorten the working day?
cases.wording: Teacher says: This is the man we call Lord Shaftesbury. He wasn't a king who could order everybody to obey him. He worked in Parliament, and he joined other people asking for changes. His campaign for a ten-hour day didn't win straight away. Some factory owners thought shorter hours would cost them money. Look at the dates. The 1833 Act protected children in particular textile factories, the factories making cloth. It wasn't the ten-hour law. Four inspectors were appointed to check whether owners followed it. Later came the ten-hour law, and then fixed times for the working day. These were steps over many years. Now, why would a law need someone to check it?

cases.subject: History
cases.beat: Had the law solved the problem?
cases.wording:
Factory inspector's report, 1836 (adapted):
Boys at Taylor, Ibbotson & Co. said they worked from Friday morning until Saturday afternoon, with breaks for meals and one extra hour at midnight. The inspector checked their accounts and said he would punish the firm.

cases.subject: History
cases.beat: Had the law solved the problem?
cases.wording: Choose the claim this report supports.

cases.subject: History
cases.beat: Had the law solved the problem?
cases.wording: A. Every factory obeyed the law.

cases.subject: History
cases.beat: Had the law solved the problem?
cases.wording: B. Some children still worked at night, and an inspector challenged the firm.

cases.subject: History
cases.beat: Had the law solved the problem?
cases.wording: C. The law had changed nothing anywhere.

cases.subject: History
cases.beat: Had the law solved the problem?
cases.wording: Teacher says: This report was written three years after the Act. The inspector spoke to the boys and checked their accounts. Decide which claim the report supports. Look carefully at what it tells us about this firm. Then ask whether it could possibly tell us what happened in every other factory as well.

cases.subject: History
cases.beat: Which children did the Mines Act protect?
cases.wording: The 1842 Mines Act banned underground work for women, girls and boys under ten.

cases.subject: History
cases.beat: Which children did the Mines Act protect?
cases.wording: Reports described children working below ground. Shaftesbury helped bring the problem before Parliament and supported the new law. Boys aged ten and over could still work underground.

cases.subject: History
cases.beat: Which children did the Mines Act protect?
cases.wording: Did the Act remove every child from the mines?

cases.subject: History
cases.beat: Which children did the Mines Act protect?
cases.wording: Teacher says: Last lesson's mine work gives us another problem to think about. These reports told Parliament about children below ground. Shaftesbury supported changing the law. Read who the new rule protected: all women and girls, and boys under ten. That's a real change for those groups. But now look at the other line. A boy aged twelve was still allowed to work underground. The law didn't make every mine safe or remove every child. We need to say exactly who it reached when we explain why the change mattered.

cases.subject: History
cases.beat: Who had to stop working underground?
cases.wording: The 1842 rule banned underground work for women, girls and boys under ten.

cases.subject: History

cases.wording: Sort the examples using the 1842 rule.

cases.subject: History

cases.wording: Banned from underground work

cases.subject: History

cases.wording: Still allowed underground

cases.subject: History
cases.beat: Who had to stop working underground?
cases.wording: A twelve-year-old boy

cases.subject: History

cases.wording: A nine-year-old boy

cases.subject: History
cases.beat: Who had to stop working underground?
cases.wording: A twelve-year-old girl

cases.subject: History
cases.beat: Who had to stop working underground?
cases.wording: Teacher says: Read the whole rule, not only the number ten. Decide where each example belongs before comparing your answers.

cases.subject: History
cases.wording: ragged schools: Ragged schools gave free lessons to children whose families had very little money.

cases.subject: History
cases.beat: Why were free schools needed too?
cases.wording: Ragged schools gave poorer children a chance to learn without paying school fees.

cases.subject: History
cases.beat: Why were free schools needed too?
cases.wording: A shorter working day didn't give a family money for school. Volunteer teachers ran free lessons, and Shaftesbury became president of the Ragged School Union in 1844. He helped support schools that others ran.

cases.subject: History
cases.beat: Why were free schools needed too?
cases.wording: What could a free school offer that a shorter working day couldn't?

cases.subject: History
cases.beat: Why were free schools needed too?
cases.wording: Ragged schools gave poorer children a chance to learn without paying school fees.

cases.subject: History
cases.beat: Why were free schools needed too?
cases.wording: Teacher says: We've talked about taking children out of some work and shortening other work. But what could they do with that time? A family might still have no money for school fees. That's where free lessons mattered. Look at this ragged school. Volunteers gave their time to teach. Shaftesbury became president of the group that supported these schools. He helped, but he wasn't the teacher in every classroom and he didn't invent every school. More time and a place to learn were different things; children could need both.

cases.subject: History
cases.beat: What did each change make possible?
cases.wording:
A family could not afford school fees. Their child stopped working underground after the Mines Act.

Did the Mines Act alone give the child a place to learn? Explain what ragged schools could add.

cases.subject: History
cases.beat: What did each change make possible?
cases.wording: Teacher says: Keep the two changes separate in your head. One was a rule about work below ground. The other offered something the family couldn't pay for. Settle your answer, then tell your partner what the free school added.

cases.subject: History
cases.wording: historically significant: We call someone historically significant when we judge that what they did mattered in history.

cases.subject: History
cases.beat: Why did people choose to remember Shaftesbury?
cases.wording: People paid for a memorial to Shaftesbury because they wanted his work to be remembered.

cases.subject: History
cases.beat: Why did people choose to remember Shaftesbury?
cases.wording: Shaftesbury died in 1885. The memorial opened in London in 1893, after his death. We judge someone historically significant by what changed, who it reached and why people remembered it later.

cases.subject: History
cases.beat: Why did people choose to remember Shaftesbury?
cases.wording: What does building this memorial tell us about the people who paid for it?

cases.subject: History
cases.beat: Why did people choose to remember Shaftesbury?
cases.wording: Teacher says: This is a memorial, something people made to remember him. He had died eight years before it opened. The people who paid for it were making a choice: they wanted his work remembered in a public place. That helps us explain why he was historically significant. We can ask what changed, who the changes reached, and whether people still thought the work mattered later. The fountain doesn't prove every child was safe. The work and the later choice to remember it are two different pieces of evidence.

cases.subject: History
cases.beat: Could someone who helped fewer children matter too?
cases.wording:
John Pounds taught more than forty children without charging fees in his Portsmouth workshop. He died in 1839. Other people took inspiration from his teaching, and a church in Portsmouth carries his name.
Modern summary from John Pounds Memorial Church.

Why might Portsmouth choose to remember John Pounds? Use what changed, who it reached and how he was remembered.

cases.subject: History
cases.beat: Could someone who helped fewer children matter too?
cases.wording: Explain <<what changed>> for children.

cases.subject: History

cases.wording: Say <<which children>> the change reached.

cases.subject: History
cases.beat: Could someone who helped fewer children matter too?
cases.wording: Explain how people chose to remember his work later.

cases.subject: History
cases.beat: Could someone who helped fewer children matter too?
cases.wording: Support your explanation with evidence.

cases.subject: History
cases.beat: Could someone who helped fewer children matter too?
cases.wording: Teacher says: Shaftesbury wasn't the only person who mattered. Here's a shoemaker who taught local children. Use the same questions we used for Shaftesbury. What could children do because the lessons were free? Who benefited? And what shows that people chose to remember John Pounds afterwards? You don't have to claim he reached as many people as a national law. Settle your own reason before talking with your partner.

cases.subject: History
cases.wording:
Why was Lord Shaftesbury historically significant?

Work: Shaftesbury supported the 1842 Mines Act. It banned underground work for women, girls and boys under ten; older boys could still work underground.

Learning: Shaftesbury supported ragged schools, where volunteer teachers gave poorer children free lessons.

New evidence: In 1944, long after his death, the charity supporting ragged schools changed its name from the Ragged School Union to the Shaftesbury Society.
Modern summary from the charity's history.

cases.subject: History
cases.wording: John Pounds mattered to poorer children in Portsmouth because his free lessons let them learn without paying fees. He taught more than forty children and inspired others. The church carrying his name shows that people wanted his work remembered.

cases.subject: History
cases.wording: John Pounds was important because he was kind and famous.

cases.subject: History
cases.wording: The strong answer says what free lessons let children do and how people remembered his work.

cases.subject: History
cases.wording: Explain how <<work and learning>> changed for children.

cases.subject: History
cases.wording: Explain what the <<1944 name change>> tells us.

cases.subject: History
cases.wording: Shaftesbury was significant because he helped change children's work and learning. He campaigned with others for factory rules and supported the Mines Act, so younger boys and girls were protected from underground work. He also supported ragged schools, where poorer children could learn without fees. The charity taking his name in 1944 shows that people still wanted his work remembered. He didn't end all child labour himself: older boys could still work underground, and some owners broke the rules.

cases.subject: History
cases.wording: Teacher says: Look at the two answers about John Pounds. The strong one explains what free lessons let children do and how people remembered his work. Find those links. Now write your own explanation about Shaftesbury. The evidence includes his work on mines and schools. There's also something new: the charity that supported ragged schools changed its name long after he died. Think about what that choice tells us.

cases.subject: History
cases.wording:
Evidence to use:
• Shaftesbury campaigned with others for factory rules and inspectors. Some owners still broke the rules.
• The 1842 Mines Act banned underground work for women, girls and boys under ten. Boys aged ten and over could still work underground.
• Shaftesbury supported ragged schools, which offered free lessons to poorer children.

New evidence: In 1944, long after his death, the charity supporting ragged schools changed its name from the Ragged School Union to the Shaftesbury Society.
Modern summary from the charity's history.

Rewrite the label so it agrees with the evidence.

Use an example about work, an example about learning and the 1944 name change.

cases.subject: Science
cases.wording:
Why do our bodies need food?

What do teeth do to food?

cases.subject: Science
cases.wording:
Food helps us get energy, grow and stay healthy.
Teeth break food into smaller pieces.

cases.subject: Science
cases.wording: Teacher says: Think about what your body does all day, even when you're sitting still. Why do our bodies need food? Now think about the bite before you swallow it. What do teeth do to food?

cases.subject: Science
cases.wording: digestive system: The digestive system is the group of body parts that breaks down food and takes useful substances from it.

cases.subject: Science
cases.wording: oesophagus: The oesophagus is the tube that carries swallowed food to the stomach.

cases.subject: Science
cases.beat: From the mouth to the stomach
cases.wording: Food enters the digestive system through the mouth.

cases.subject: Science
cases.beat: From the mouth to the stomach
cases.wording: Teeth break food into smaller pieces. Saliva wets it, and the oesophagus pushes swallowed food towards the stomach.

cases.subject: Science
cases.beat: From the mouth to the stomach
cases.wording: Which part connects the mouth to the stomach?

cases.subject: Science
cases.beat: From the mouth to the stomach
cases.wording: Teacher says: You remembered that teeth break food into smaller pieces. That happens in your mouth, so digestion has already started before you swallow. The wet liquid in your mouth is saliva. It helps make the food easier to swallow. Look at the long tube below the mouth. That's the oesophagus. Follow it down: it joins the mouth to the stomach. Food doesn't drop into an empty space inside you. The tube pushes it along. These connected parts belong to the digestive system.

cases.subject: Science
cases.wording: Name the parts marked A and B.

cases.subject: Science
cases.wording: Teacher says: Look at where each line ends. Name the parts marked A and B. Think of the opening where food enters and the tube that carries it after swallowing.

cases.subject: Science
cases.wording: The stomach churns food and mixes it with digestive juices, including acid.

cases.subject: Science
cases.wording: The oesophagus ends in this stretchy bag. Food stays here for a while before moving into the intestine.

cases.subject: Science
cases.wording: Where does the oesophagus open?

cases.subject: Science
cases.wording: The stomach churns food and mixes it with digestive juices, including acid.

cases.subject: Science
cases.wording: Teacher says: Follow the oesophagus to its end. It opens into this bag-shaped part: the stomach. People sometimes call the whole front of their body their tummy, but the stomach is this one organ. Its muscular walls squeeze and mix the food. Digestive juices, including acid, help break the food down. It doesn't finish its journey here. There's another opening where the partly digested food moves on.

cases.subject: Science
cases.wording: small intestine / large intestine: The small intestine is the narrow, coiled tube where useful nutrients from digested food pass into the blood. The large intestine is the wider tube that absorbs water from the waste left over.

cases.subject: Science
cases.wording: Food moves through the small intestine before the large intestine.

cases.subject: Science
cases.wording: The narrow coils take useful nutrients into the blood. The wider tube absorbs water from what is left.

cases.subject: Science
cases.wording: Which tube is coiled inside the other?

cases.subject: Science
cases.wording: Food moves through the small intestine before the large intestine.

cases.subject: Science
cases.wording: Teacher says: The stomach opens into the small intestine. Look at how this narrow tube coils up inside the body. Useful nutrients from digested food pass through its wall into the blood. Nutrients are useful substances your body needs. Now follow the route into the wider tube around the outside. That's the large intestine. It absorbs water from the waste that's left. Small and large describe the width of these tubes; the small intestine is actually longer. 'Small' is doing a rather misleading job in that name! What matters on this picture is the narrow coils inside and the wider tube around them.

cases.subject: Science
cases.wording: Name C and D, then show which one food reaches first.

cases.subject: Science
cases.wording: Teacher says: Name C and D, then show which one food reaches first. Follow from the stomach, rather than deciding from the size of the space each tube fills.

cases.subject: Science
cases.wording: Waste is stored in the rectum and leaves the body through the anus.

cases.subject: Science
cases.wording: The rectum is at the end of the large intestine. The anus is the opening out of the body.

cases.subject: Science

cases.subject: Science
cases.wording: Teacher says: We've followed the food all the way to the large intestine. The waste doesn't stay there for ever. At the end is the rectum, where waste is stored until you go to the toilet. Then it leaves through an opening called the anus. These are the proper names for two different parts: the rectum stores the waste; the anus is the opening. This diagram shows the usual route through the body.
